before: This is the sudden medical emergency defense, and it exists in both Georgia and South Carolina. When it works, the driver who caused the crash may owe you nothing. But the defense has limits, and it fails more often than you might think. Whether you were hurt in a car accident, a pedestrian collision, or a motorcycle crash caused by a medically impaired driver, your right to compensation depends on the specific facts and which state's law applies. The sudden emergency doctrine is well-established across American tort law, but Georgia and South Carolina apply it differently.
after: This is the sudden medical emergency defense, and it exists in both Georgia and South Carolina. When it works, the driver who caused the crash may owe you nothing. But the defense has limits, and it fails more often than you might think. Whether you were hurt in a car accident, a pedestrian collision, or a motorcycle crash caused by a medically impaired driver, your right to compensation depends on the specific facts and which state's law applies. Courts in both states treat a sudden, unforeseeable loss of consciousness as distinct from the broader sudden emergency doctrine about reacting to a peril, and Georgia and South Carolina apply the same rule within different comparative-fault and filing-deadline frameworks.

before: Georgia courts have consistently held that a driver who knows about a medical condition that could impair their ability to drive safely has a duty to refrain from driving or take reasonable precautions. Under Georgia's general negligence principles, every driver owes a duty of ordinary care to others on the road. A driver who gets behind the wheel despite knowing they could lose consciousness has breached that duty.
after: Georgia courts limit the defense to an unforeseeable loss of consciousness; a driver who had warning of the condition cannot rely on it (Eatmon v. Weeks, Ga. App. 2013). Under Georgia's general negligence principles, every driver owes a duty of ordinary care to others on the road. A driver who gets behind the wheel despite knowing they could lose consciousness has breached that duty.

before:
Georgia courts have addressed the sudden medical emergency defense in several key decisions. In cases where the driver had no prior history of the medical condition, courts have allowed the defense to go to the jury. But where evidence showed the driver had experienced prior episodes, had been warned by a doctor, or had failed to take prescribed medication, Georgia courts have rejected the defense or allowed the jury to weigh those facts against the claim of unforeseeability.

Georgia's driver licensing statutes under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-1 et seq. also play a role. Drivers have an obligation to meet fitness standards for licensure. A driver whose medical condition renders them unfit to drive safely may face additional liability exposure if they continued driving despite medical advice to stop.
after:
Georgia courts have addressed the sudden medical emergency defense in several key decisions. In cases where the driver had no prior history of the medical condition, courts have allowed the defense to go to the jury or granted the driver summary judgment outright. But where evidence showed the driver had experienced prior episodes, had been warned by a doctor, or had failed to take prescribed medication, Georgia courts have rejected the defense or allowed the jury to weigh those facts against the claim of unforeseeability.

Georgia's driver licensing law also plays a role. Under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35, physicians may report a person whose disability makes safe driving impossible to the Department of Driver Services, which may revoke or refuse a license on medical grounds after notice and a hearing; state licensing rules set a six-month seizure-free standard. A driver whose medical condition renders them unfit to drive safely may face additional liability exposure if they continued driving despite medical advice to stop.

before: Even when the sudden medical emergency defense is raised, Georgia's modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 still applies. Georgia follows a less than 50% bar — you can recover damages as long as your own fault is less than 50% of the total. If a jury finds that you were partially at fault for the accident (for example, you were speeding or not wearing a seatbelt), your damages are reduced by your percentage of fault.

before: Personal injury claims in Georgia must be filed within 2 years of the date of the accident under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. This deadline applies regardless of whether the sudden medical emergency defense is involved. If the crash resulted in a death, wrongful death claims also carry a 2-year filing deadline in Georgia.

before: Like Georgia, South Carolina places the burden on the defendant to establish the sudden medical emergency defense. The driver must show that they suffered an unforeseeable medical event that rendered them incapable of controlling their vehicle. South Carolina courts evaluate foreseeability based on the totality of the circumstances, including the driver's medical history, any prior episodes, doctor's warnings, and medication compliance.
after: Like Georgia, South Carolina places the burden on the defendant to establish the sudden medical emergency defense. The driver must show that they suffered an unforeseeable medical event that rendered them incapable of controlling their vehicle. South Carolina courts ask whether the incapacity was unforeseeable, looking at the driver's medical history, any prior episodes, treating-physician testimony, and medication effects (Collins v. Frasier, S.C. Ct. App. 2008).

before: South Carolina's vehicle fitness and licensing requirements under S.C. Code § 56-5-6110 et seq. further reinforce the expectation that drivers maintain physical fitness for safe vehicle operation. Violations of these provisions can serve as evidence of negligence independent of the sudden emergency analysis.
after: South Carolina's licensing law, including S.C. Code § 56-1-221, which creates the SCDMV Medical Advisory Board, further reinforces the expectation that drivers maintain physical fitness for safe vehicle operation. A driver's licensing history and any medical restrictions on the license are evidence of what the driver knew.

If the jury finds the medically impaired driver was 55% at fault (perhaps because they should have known about the risk) and you were 45% at fault, you would recover 55% of your damages in South Carolina but would be completely barred in Georgia.
after: In a medical emergency accident case, this distinction can matter. If the jury finds you and the medically impaired driver each 50% at fault (perhaps because the driver should have known about the risk), you would recover 50% of your damages in South Carolina but would be completely barred in Georgia.

before: South Carolina gives injured victims 3 years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. This extra year compared to Georgia provides more time to investigate the at-fault driver's medical history, obtain medical records through discovery, and build a case that the medical emergency was foreseeable.

before: A doctor who prescribed medication with known side effects that impair driving ability — and failed to warn the patient about those risks — may be liable for medical malpractice. Similarly, a physician who cleared a patient to drive despite knowing about a condition that made driving dangerous could face liability. These claims require proving that the doctor's conduct fell below the applicable standard of care.
after: Whether the driver's doctor can be liable depends on the state. In South Carolina, a medical provider who gives treatment it knows may impair the patient's abilities owes a duty to warn the patient, and reasonably foreseeable third parties can sue when it does not (Hardee v. Bio Medical Applications of South Carolina, Inc., S.C. 2006). Georgia courts have refused to extend a physician's duty to third parties injured by a patient who drove after treatment (Gilhuly v. Dockery, Ga. App. 2005). Where the claim exists, it is closely related to medical malpractice and requires proving that the provider's conduct fell below the applicable standard of care.

before: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires commercial driver's license (CDL) holders to pass a physical examination every two years. Conditions like epilepsy, insulin-dependent diabetes (without an exemption), and certain cardiac conditions can disqualify a driver. An employer who ignored these requirements or failed to verify its drivers' medical certifications may be negligent.
after: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires interstate commercial drivers to be medically examined and certified at least every 24 months (49 CFR 391.45). Conditions like epilepsy, certain cardiac conditions, and insulin-treated diabetes that is not managed under FMCSA's assessment-form process (49 CFR 391.46, which replaced the old exemption program in 2018) can disqualify a driver. An employer who ignored these requirements or failed to verify its drivers' medical certifications may be negligent.

before: Both Georgia and South Carolina require insurers to offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage. UM/UIM coverage protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance, insufficient insurance, or — in some interpretations — when the at-fault driver is found not liable and you cannot recover from their policy. Whether UM/UIM applies when the other driver is found not liable due to a sudden emergency defense depends on the specific policy language and the state's case law. An experienced attorney can evaluate whether your UM/UIM coverage provides a path to recovery.
after: Both Georgia and South Carolina require insurers to offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage. UM/UIM pays what you are legally entitled to recover from the other driver (S.C. Code § 38-77-150; O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11). If the driver is found not negligent because of a sudden, unforeseeable incapacity, UM/UIM generally does not pay either; it is the remedy when the defense fails and the driver is uninsured or underinsured. An experienced attorney can evaluate whether your UM/UIM coverage provides a path to recovery.

before: South Carolina requires PIP coverage as part of every auto insurance policy. PIP pays for your medical expenses and lost wages regardless of who was at fault. Georgia does not mandate PIP, but some Georgia drivers carry it as an optional add-on. PIP benefits are typically limited in amount but provide immediate coverage while you pursue other claims.
after: Neither state requires PIP. South Carolina law says so expressly (S.C. Code § 38-77-144), and Georgia has no PIP mandate; Georgia's optional first-party coverage is sold as medical payments coverage. If you bought optional PIP, it pays for your medical expenses and lost wages regardless of who was at fault. PIP benefits are typically limited in amount but provide immediate coverage while you pursue other claims.

This is especially important when the driver's defense succeeds, because these alternative defendants may be your primary source of recovery.

before: The sudden medical emergency defense allows drivers to avoid liability for accidents caused by unforeseeable medical events like heart attacks, seizures, and strokes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, the burden falls on the driver to prove the episode was genuinely unforeseeable. The defense fails when the driver had prior episodes, doctor's warnings, or untreated conditions. Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) apply. Even if the defense succeeds, injured victims may recover through UM/UIM coverage, PIP, MedPay, or claims against prescribing physicians.
after: The sudden medical emergency defense allows drivers to avoid liability for accidents caused by unforeseeable medical events like heart attacks, seizures, and strokes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, the burden falls on the driver to prove the episode was genuinely unforeseeable. The defense fails when the driver had prior episodes, doctor's warnings, or untreated conditions. Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) apply. Even if the defense succeeds, coverage that pays regardless of fault (MedPay, optional PIP, health insurance) may still apply, and in South Carolina a medical provider who failed to warn the driver about impairing treatment may be liable; Georgia does not recognize that claim. UM/UIM applies when the driver is liable but uninsured or underinsured.

Uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage pays only what you are legally entitled to recover from the other driver, so it applies when the driver is liable but uninsured or underinsured.
